outcome: Hegde, Sandeep and Shashank proved the conjecture for P13-free graphs (arXiv:2410.22842, first posted 2024-10-30), a case settlement; Carr's diameter-2 result is a second case. [Hand-corrected 2026-09-28; the agent's original outcome follows.] The general conjecture (every graph of minimum degree ≥3 contains a cycle of power-of-two length) remains open, but since the frozen revision several genuine advances have occurred: the conjecture was proved for P13-free graphs (Feb 2025) and for diameter-2 minimum-degree-3 graphs (Aug 2025/Jan 2026); and the best known lower bound on the order of a minimal counterexample was pushed from 17 to 24 (Sept 2026, with disclosed Claude assistance) and, for the cubic bipartite case, from 30 to 60 (Aug 2026, with disclosed ChatGPT/Codex assistance) via certified SAT/exhaustive computation.

summary: The Erdős–Gyárfás conjecture (every graph of minimum degree ≥3 has a cycle whose length is a power of 2) remains open in general as of 2026-09-22. Since the frozen revision (2024-01-26), the conjecture has been confirmed for additional restricted graph classes: P13-free graphs (Hegde, Sandeep, Shashank, arXiv:2410.22842, first posted 2024-10-30, revised 2025-02-11, via a C++ backtracking/brute-force search, no AI disclosed), and graphs of diameter 2 with minimum degree ≥3 (Carr, arXiv:2508.19302, posted 2025-08-25, published 2026-01-30, no AI disclosed) — both are cases of the general conjecture under §3.1, so `partial` progress, confirming the conjecture on the restricted classes. Separately (and this is the more interesting AI-relevant thread), the literature on lower bounds for a minimal counterexample's order has moved substantially in 2026: arXiv:2609.04686 (Daniel Garcia, posted 2026-09-04) raises the general minimum-degree-3 bound from 17 to 24 vertices via a SAT-based exhaustive search certified by DRAT proofs, and explicitly states 'Computations were carried out with the assistance of an AI system (Claude); all results were independently re-verified' — the independent re-verification (two separate cycle-detection procedures, DRAT certification via drat-trim) means the mathematical certificate itself is machine-checkable and not merely an AI assertion, but Claude's assistance went into producing the computational/structural work, not just checking it, so I code this `bound`/AI-assisted rather than `none`. arXiv:2608.02675 (Julius Tranquilli, posted 2026-08-02) raises the cubic-bipartite bound from 30 to 60 vertices, with an explicit 'AI disclosure' section crediting OpenAI ChatGPT with 'developing computational and structural approaches, portions of the incidence-based code and preliminary arguments' and OpenAI Codex with code auditing and manuscript drafting — again the underlying claim rests on independently-checked certificates (two independently implemented C16 oracles plus a static witness certificate), but substantial mathematical/structural work was AI-assisted per the authors' own account. Both authors appear to be independent researchers (Tranquilli is a formal-methods/software engineer per his personal site and Google Scholar, not a professional mathematician) rather than academic specialists, which is itself notable: SAT-based bound-improvement work on this conjecture, previously the province of specialists (Royle & Markström ~2004), is now being done by AI-assisted individual researchers. None of these results settle the conjecture — they narrow where a counterexample could be, which per §3.1's rule for existence-type problems ('are there infinitely many X') would not normally count, but the bullet in question is specifically an existence/universal-quantifier statement, not a record-table question, so I classify the bound-improvement papers under `ai_role: bound` (an AI system moved a bound on a problem that is still open) while keeping overall `status: progress` rather than `partial`, since the decisive event I am dating (2609.04686) is a bound movement, not a case-settlement. The P13-free and diameter-2 results are real `partial`-type progress but are not the AI story here and are not disclosed as AI-assisted, so they support `status` moving off `open` independently of the AI angle. I checked erdosproblems.com's Problem #64 page, which confirms Liu–Montgomery's large-minimum-degree resolution (JAMS 2023) predates the window entirely and is not new. I also checked the Machine Intelligence Research Institute's May 2026 'The Erdős Proof and AI Capabilities' post, which discusses an OpenAI-internal model disproving the Erdős unit distance conjecture — unrelated to Erdős–Gyárfás, and not relevant here despite superficially similar naming.
competing_reading: One could argue `status` should be `partial` rather than `progress`, treating the P13-free and diameter-2 results (each a genuine case of the general conjecture, confirming it) as the decisive events, with the AI-assisted bound papers relegated to a `progress` note in summary. I chose `progress` with the September 2026 bound paper as the decisive event because it is the most recent and, per the brief, the AI angle is the more analytically interesting thread; but a reader treating 'has a case been settled' as automatically taking precedence over 'has a bound moved' would file this as `partial` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (for the P13-free/diameter-2 classes) and record the bound papers only in summary. Also debatable: whether Claude/ChatGPT's role in the bound papers rises to `assisted` (mathematics in the result) rather than `bound` — I used `bound` because the underlying open problem is still open and what moved is explicitly a numeric bound, matching §6.2's `bound` code more precisely than `assisted`, but the authors' language ('developing computational and structural approaches... preliminary arguments') sounds like it satisfies `assisted`'s bar too; the two codes are not mutually exclusive in the taxonomy's spirit and I picked `bound` as the more specific/informative code per the guidance that `bound` is for moving a number on a still-open problem.
what_would_settle_it: A clearer breakdown from the authors (or a third-party digestion) of exactly which lines of code, which lemmas, or which parts of the 'window calculus' / 'triangle-rooted method' were AI-produced versus human-produced would resolve whether `bound` or `assisted` is the better fit. A future paper actually resolving the conjecture (or disproving it) would supersede this record entirely.
